sections.h2: What should a Tennessee home seller know about the state first?
sections.html:
Tennessee is a state of 7,315,076 residents, according to the Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate, up 5.8 percent from the April 2020 base. The Census QuickFacts table counts 3,291,207 housing units, an owner-occupied rate of 66.9 percent for 2020 to 2024 and a median owner-occupied value of $286,700. Median gross rent is $1,189.

Those statewide numbers hide wide gaps between a Memphis block, a Nashville suburb and a Smoky Mountain county seat. The guides in this directory break the state into county level and city level pages so a seller can find the register of deeds, the property tax rules and the local selling steps for one address instead of an average.

sections.h2: How is Tennessee divided into counties and cities?
sections.html:
The state has 95 counties, each with a county seat, and 340 municipalities, based on Wikipedia's summary of Tennessee. The state is also split into three Grand Divisions: East, Middle and West Tennessee. Davidson County (Nashville), Moore County (Lynchburg) and Trousdale County (Hartsville) have governments consolidated with their county seats.

Every county elects a sheriff, property assessor, trustee, register of deeds and county clerk. That list is useful for a seller, because each of those offices answers a different closing question.

  • The assessor appraises the house and keeps ownership and boundary records.
  • The trustee collects county property tax.
  • The register of deeds records the deed and collects the recordation tax.
  • The county clerk handles records that sit outside those three offices.

sections.h2: Where do Tennessee's biggest markets sit?
sections.html:
Nashville is both capital and largest city, and its 13 county metropolitan area holds about 2 million residents. Memphis passed 630,000 residents and sits in Shelby County, the largest county by population and land area. The Tri-Cities of Kingsport, Bristol and Johnson City form what Wikipedia calls the sixth major population center.

sections.h2: How does Tennessee property tax work for a seller?
sections.html:
Assessment and taxation are separate jobs. The Comptroller explains that the county assessor appraises and classifies property, the county commission and city governing bodies set the rates, and the county trustee and city officials collect the bill. Residential and farm property are assessed at 25 percent of appraised value, commercial and industrial at 40 percent, public utility property at 55 percent and business personal property at 30 percent.

Reappraisals run on 6, 5 or 4 year cycles, and the assessor mails an Assessment Change Notice when a value or classification changes. An appeal can rest on a value that is too high, another owner's value that is too low, or the wrong classification. The County Board of Equalization meets beginning June 1, with the State Board of Equalization and Chancery Court beyond it. Each county guide in this directory covers its own offices and dates.

sections.h2: What property tax relief exists for Tennessee homeowners?
sections.html:
The Comptroller's Property Tax Programs page lists two programs. State law provides relief for low-income elderly and disabled homeowners and for disabled veteran homeowners or their surviving spouses. A separate tax freeze holds the property taxes on a principal residence at a base amount, which is the tax owed in the year the owner first qualifies.

If you are selling a home that has been in a relief or freeze program, ask the county trustee how the program ends at a sale and what balance remains. The trustee is also the office that takes the final payment before closing.

sections.h2: What taxes does Tennessee charge on a home sale?
sections.html:
The state has no individual income tax on wages or most other income, and the Hall tax on interest and dividends was repealed for tax periods beginning January 1, 2021 or later. The main state cost on a sale is the realty transfer tax, which the Department of Revenue sets at $0.37 per $100 of purchase price. The grantee pays it to the register of deeds.

Wikipedia notes that property taxes are the primary revenue source for local governments and that the sales tax is the main source for the state. Federal tax on any gain is a separate matter, covered in our capital gains and estate guides.

sections.h2: Which landlord and tenant rules vary across Tennessee?
sections.html:
Rental rules depend on the county. A Tennessee Courts judicial academy presentation lists nineteen counties that follow the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, from Anderson and Blount to Williamson and Wilson, while every other county falls under Title 66, Chapter 7. URLTA counties give tenants a five day grace period and cap late fees at 10 percent.

A seller with a tenant in the house should check which set of rules applies before any notice goes out. Our eviction notice guide lays out the notice periods and the detainer warrant steps for both groups of counties.

sections.h2: How does Tennessee weather affect an older house?
sections.html:
Most of the state has a humid subtropical climate with about 50 inches of precipitation a year. Tornadoes are possible throughout Tennessee, with West and Middle Tennessee the most vulnerable, and the state averages 15 a year. Ice storms are fairly common, and fog is a persistent problem in parts of East Tennessee.

Roof age, drainage and tree limbs near the house deserve a look before a sale. Ask the county assessor whether storm repairs or an addition have changed the property record, because the assessor tracks changes to buildings between reappraisals.

sections.h2: How should I use these Tennessee guides?
sections.html:
Pick the guide that matches the address. County pages cover register of deeds offices for places such as Shelby, Knox, Hamilton, Davidson, Williamson and Sumner. Property tax guides cover many of the larger counties and cities. City pages walk through selling a house in Nashville, Memphis, Knoxville, Chattanooga, Clarksville, Murfreesboro and other Tennessee cities.

Statewide topics round out the set, including property tax appeals, homestead exemption, estate and inheritance tax, quitclaim deeds, transfer on death deeds, capital gains tax and eviction notices. Start with the topic that fits your situation, then move to the county page for your parcel.

faqs.q: How many counties does Tennessee have?
faqs.a: Ninety-five, each with a county seat. Davidson, Moore and Trousdale counties have governments consolidated with their seats.

faqs.q: Which Tennessee office records a deed?
faqs.a: The county register of deeds. That office also collects the recordation tax, which includes the realty transfer tax of $0.37 per $100 of purchase price.

faqs.q: How is a Tennessee house assessed for property tax?
faqs.a: The county assessor applies a 25 percent assessment ratio to the appraised value of residential property. A home appraised at $100,000 has an assessed value of $25,000, and the local tax rate is applied to that figure.

faqs.q: Does Tennessee have a state income tax on home sale profits?
faqs.a: No. The Department of Revenue says Tennessee has no individual income tax on wages or most other income, and its Hall tax on interest and dividends was repealed for periods beginning January 1, 2021 or later.

faqs.q: Where can I find the rules for a county I do not see here?
faqs.a: Ask the register of deeds, assessor or trustee in that county, and check the Tennessee Comptroller's Division of Property Assessments pages for assessment cycles and appeal steps.
